84 Marlborough Street, Cathedral Street, Dublin 1, DUBLIN
candidates.description_override: Corner-sited three-bay three-storey house over basement, built c.1795, with recent replacement shopfronts to both elevations. Slated M-profile roof with shared rebuilt brick chimneystacks behind granite-capped parapet to (east) elevation, hipped to north elevation. Eaves dressed in copper and cast-iron rainwater goods to each end of side elevation. Red brick walls laid in Flemish bond to north façade, having corbel brick eaves course and elliptical cast-iron tie-plates between floors. Two-bay east elevation with red brick walls laid in Flemish bond rebuilt above second floor windows having granite capped parapet. Gauged flat-arch window openings having brick reveals and granite sills and having two-over-two timber sliding sash windows throughout. Round-arch door opening with open-pedimented stucco surround and brick relieving arch. Painted timber replacement panelled door with narrow overlight below plain glass fanlight having original wrought-iron security bars behind. Reproduction shopfront to west of north elevation having evidence of original brick flat-arched window opening over. Contemporary shopfront to east having three-light display window. North elevation having principal shopfront in contemporary style over basement area enclosed by replacement chamfered granite plinth and replacement railings with matching gate and steps. Door opens onto single moulded step on building line to platform at street level.
candidates.significance_override: The NIAH appraisal describes the recently restored townhouse as well presented and notes that its scale and contemporary shopfronts contribute to the early streets and provide an appropriate setting for the Pro-Cathedral opposite.

candidates.official_page_title: The Confession Box, 88 Marlborough Street, Dublin 1, DUBLIN

candidates.significance_override: The NIAH appraisal notes that Marlborough Street was opened around 1700 by the Moore family, Earls of Drogheda. The graduated fenestration and plot ratio suggest an early nineteenth-century date, while the stucco decoration indicates a later nineteenth-century overhaul. Its decorative façade and pedimented doorcases contribute to the street's historic character.

candidates.official_page_title: Dunnes Stores, 23–24 Earl Street North / Cathedral Street, Dublin 1, DUBLIN
candidates.significance_override: The NIAH appraisal places the building within the commercial streetscape around O'Connell Street. Its Earl Street elevation belongs to the rebuilding that followed the 1916 Rising, while the rear block and later reconstruction contribute to the area's layered commercial fabric.
